title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
author: Anonymous
openingText: Let the one who has tested the heart of all things teach the nation. Let the one who holds all knowledge school all the people; let him pass on his wisdom so that they share it together. Gilgamesh was that master of wisdom, who knew all things. He was the one who uncovered what was hidden. He handed down the tradition of the days before the Flood. He went on a far journey, came back weary and worn by his labour, and carved the whole of his hardship on a tablet of stone.
about:
The Epic of Gilgamesh follows a king of Uruk, probably a real ruler of that Mesopotamian city, through friendship, grief and a search for life without death. Gilgamesh begins as a tyrant who leaves no son to his father and no bride to her husband. The gods answer the people's complaint by shaping Enkidu from clay on the open plain, a wild man who grazes with the gazelles until a courtesan brings him to the city. The two fight in the street, become brothers, and set out for the Cedar Forest to destroy its guardian, Humbaba. Gilgamesh then refuses the goddess Ishtar, and the two friends kill the Bull of Heaven she sends against him. Enkidu dreams that the gods have condemned him, falls sick and dies. Gilgamesh, terrified of death, crosses the mountains by the Road of the Sun, meets the wine-maker Siduri at the edge of the sea, and is ferried over the Waters of Death to Utnapishtim, the one man the gods made immortal. Utnapishtim tells him the story of the Flood, then shows him that he cannot even stay awake for a week. A plant of youth is found and lost to a snake. Gilgamesh comes home and shows the boatman the walls of Uruk.

The standard version of the poem took shape late in the second millennium BCE from older Sumerian and Babylonian stories. Its best-preserved copies were found in the 1850s in the ruins of Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, written on twelve clay tablets in the seventh century BCE. Many lines are still broken.

This edition is the translation the British Assyriologist R. Campbell Thompson published in 1928, made from his own collation of the tablets in the British Museum and set in English hexameters. Where the Nineveh tablets break off, Thompson fills the gaps with older Old Babylonian tablets, so a few scenes are told twice and some passages stop at a gap. The fight with Humbaba itself survives only in a Hittite version that this edition leaves out: Tablet V passes from the dreams on the road to the moment the heroes cut off Humbaba's head.

angleCards.title: The first answer to mortality.
angleCards.text: Gilgamesh is four thousand years old and still asks the question we ask. Watch how the poem refuses easy consolation, and what it quietly offers instead.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how one of the oldest stories ever written treats the problem of mortality, and what it concludes.

angleCards.title: Friendship as the hinge of everything.
angleCards.text: Enkidu and Gilgamesh become equals in a way neither expected. The second half of the epic exists because one of them dies. Notice how grief becomes fear, and fear becomes a journey.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read this as a story about friendship: what it means to have a true equal, and what grief does to a person when that equal is gone.

angleCards.title: Wild vs. civilised.
angleCards.text: Enkidu begins among the gazelles and learns bread, beer, clothes and the city. On his deathbed he curses the woman who taught him, then blesses her. The poem keeps asking what civilisation gives and what it costs.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the tension between wildness and civilisation: what Enkidu gains and loses when he enters the city.

angleCards.title: Reading a broken text.
angleCards.text: Thompson prints the gaps. Some tablets stop mid-sentence, some scenes survive twice in older versions. Reading Gilgamesh means noticing what has been lost and what still holds together.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Gilgamesh as a text that survived in pieces, and notice how the story still carries across its gaps.

cast.name: Gilgamesh
cast.description: King of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third man. The people of his city cry out against him until the gods send him an equal. With Enkidu he goes to the Cedar Forest and kills the Bull of Heaven. When Enkidu dies he puts on animal skins, crosses the mountains and the Waters of Death to ask Utnapishtim about life and death, and comes home with nothing but the walls of Uruk to show the boatman.

cast.name: Enkidu
cast.description: Shaped by the goddess Aruru from clay on the open plain to be Gilgamesh's match. He grazes with the gazelles and frees animals from the hunter's traps until a courtesan teaches him bread, beer and the ways of the city. He blocks Gilgamesh's path in the street, wrestles him, and becomes his brother. After the Bull of Heaven he dreams that the gods have condemned him, and dies of a fever.

cast.name: Ishtar
cast.description: The goddess of Uruk. When Gilgamesh comes back from the forest and washes, she asks him to be her bridegroom and promises him a chariot of lapis and gold. He answers with a list of the lovers she ruined: Tammuz, a bird, a lion, a stallion, a shepherd, her father's gardener. In her rage she has Anu make the Bull of Heaven, and mourns over it when the two friends kill it.

cast.name: Utnapishtim
cast.description: The man of Shuruppak whom the god Ea warned of the Flood through the wall of a reed hut. He built a boat, survived the storm, and was made like the gods, to live in the distance where the rivers meet the sea. He tells Gilgamesh the whole story, then sets him a test: stay awake for six days and seven nights. Gilgamesh falls asleep at once.

cast.name: Siduri
cast.description: A veiled wine-maker who lives by the sea at the end of Gilgamesh's journey. She bars her door when she sees him in his animal skins. Then she tells him the gods kept life for themselves, and that he should fill his belly, wash, wear fresh clothes, care for the child who holds his hand and make his wife happy. She also tells him the way to Utnapishtim's boatman.

cast.name: Shamash
cast.description: The sun god and Gilgamesh's protector. Gilgamesh and his mother Ninsun pray to him before the journey to the Cedar Forest. When Enkidu curses the courtesan on his deathbed, Shamash reminds him of the bread, the clothes and the friend she gave him, and Enkidu's anger is calmed. On the far side of the mountains he asks Gilgamesh why he is running, when he will not find the life he is looking for.

acclaim.quote: Gilgamesh is stupendous! ... I consider it to be among the greatest things that can happen to a person.
acclaim.context: letter to Katharina Kippenberg, 11 December 1916, after reading Arthur Ungnad's German translation

whyItMatters.title: The Oldest Story That Still Works
whyItMatters.body: Gilgamesh is one of the oldest works of literature that survive. Its concerns are losing a close friend, fearing one's own death, hunting for a way to live for ever and coming home without it, and they are recognisable across four thousand years. The tablets were dug out of Nineveh in the 1850s, and in 1872 George Smith of the British Museum announced that one of them told of a flood, a boat and birds sent out to find land, close to the story of Noah in Genesis. Reading it shows that these questions were asked, in a finished literary form, long before Homer.

whyItMatters.title: The First Great Friendship
whyItMatters.body: The gods make Enkidu as Gilgamesh's equal, and the poem takes their bond seriously from the start: Gilgamesh dreams of him before they meet, they wrestle until the walls shake, and they go into danger together. When Enkidu dies, Gilgamesh covers his friend's face like a bride's, roars like a lioness robbed of her cubs and tears out his own hair. His grief turns into fear of his own death, and that fear drives the rest of the epic.

whyItMatters.title: The Failure of the Quest
whyItMatters.body: Gilgamesh travels to the end of the world to find life without death. He meets the one man who has it and learns that it was granted once and will not be granted again. He cannot stay awake for a week. Utnapishtim tells him of a thorny plant at the bottom of the sea that makes an old man young; he dives for it, and while he bathes in a pool a snake carries it off. He weeps, goes home, and tells the boatman to walk on the ramparts of Uruk and look at the brickwork. What the poem offers instead of immortality is what people build, and the city that outlasts its king.
